extracted.intended_audience: magicians/performers (prestidigitation), theatrical stage designers, and card-players concerned with cheating
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for staging and running prestidigitation/theatrical magic shows and for detecting and defending against card‑cheating methods (marked decks, secret signalling, deck substitution). Includes principles of presentation, apparatus design, reliability, publicity, and assistant selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disclosure vs. public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give step-by-step instructions for criminal cheating methods even when warning the public about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author refuses to specify the exact method for printing the matte point on cards: 'je me permettrai de ne pas l’indiquer, car mon but est de signaler une fourberie et non d’enseigner à la faire.' Balance is advised: inform people to recognize and avoid danger, but avoid teaching techniques that would facilitate crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting subtle card markings (matte points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marked white-backed cards can carry an almost invisible matte point that appears or disappears depending on viewing distance/angle and light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine backs with the eye and a good loupe; view from varying distances and angles to reveal matte vs. shiny differences. The text demonstrates dividing the card into vertical (8) and horizontal (4) regions to map a single point to a specific rank and suit—use a consistent spatial code to reason about any isolated spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing symmetric/tarot marking schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tarot-style backs with symmetric points can be exploited: a base point indicates suit and a secondary small point placed at one of eight positions around it indicates rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect the standard positions of the tarot design; if a small extra mark is added at one of the eight compass locations around a design point, that encodes the card (example: top = as, rotate right = roi, etc.). Be aware of many possible combinations and variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting marks via wear, cuts, or edge nicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks are not always added ink/paint; they can be produced by cutting/attacking the printed design or by tiny nicks on the edge (morfil) made during play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect card edges and printed designs for non-uniform wear or cut marks; watch for cards that can be recognized by touch or brief glance when fanned. Anti-pattern: assuming only ink marks exist and ignoring physical alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of imperceptible telegraphy (confederate signalling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Escrocs may use imperceptible, principled signalling between partners to convey an opponent’s hand without apparent communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be vigilant for subtle patterns of behaviour between players (posture, touch, routine gestures). Treat absence of obvious signals as no guarantee of safety; consider seat placement and observation of who exchanges glances or makes recurring micro-movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify chain of custody for purchased decks
rubrics_metrics.description: Decks can be marked after leaving the printer via a chain of tricks involving merchants who exchange sealed packs after returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not blindly trust a retailer’s practice of resealing/exchanging packs; establish trusted suppliers, purchase and retain your own sealed packs, and avoid letting packages circulate unattended. Example anti-pattern: buying several times to make acquaintance then returning sealed packs that get exchanged after being tampered with overnight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance 'address' (skill) and 'mechanics' (automata) in a show
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful séance should combine manual dexterity (prestidigitation) and mechanical displays (automata) so that one relieves and enhances the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program the evening so automata and sleight-of-hand alternate; use mechanical pieces to give variety and rest the audience between feats of manual skill. The two characters should complement, not compete, for audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer elegant, simple stage apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid cluttered, obvious, or crude-looking devices (e.g. huge metal lids called 'Pallas') that make the stage resemble a trinket shop rather than a magician's cabinet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design apparatus in crystal (opaque or transparent as needed) or otherwise refined forms so instruments are consonant with the aesthetic of the performance. Simplicity and elegance increase illusion and respect for the artist; anti-pattern: an overabundance of varnished metal boxes that reveal technique rather than mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize concealed mechanical substitutes that steal the artist’s credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overuse of double‑bottom boxes and instruments whose secret functions make the effect the work of a tinsmith rather than an artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true prestidigitation 'ne doit pas être l’œuvre d’un ferblantier'—present effects where the artist's skill, rather than hidden machinery, feels primary. Use mechanical aids sparingly and in ways that support, rather than replace, demonstrable skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit reliance on compères/assistants for the illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make compères perform the essential hidden work of the trick; the artist should be seen as the author of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress or reduce the role of confederates whose visible actions do the trick for the performer. This preserves the audience’s perception that the magician is the agent of the wonder and avoids the impression of a staged hand‑off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure reliability of effects and prepare contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain spectacular effects (e.g., ignition via static/electricity) are not infallible; a failure leaves the operator in an embarrassing position and ruins perceived omnipotence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test and rehearse complex, fragile effects extensively; have fallback moves or explanations to avoid 'fiasco' if a mechanism fails. The performer must avoid public situations where a promised effect cannot be delivered without losing prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity, incentives and novelty to build an audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success may depend as much on marketing as on merit: Talon used lotteries, free candies, and promised surprises to fill houses and make the show succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine reasonable admission incentives (small extras, chance to win a large prize) with novelty in the bill to attract initial crowds; once the audience is present, a pleasantly presented performance and promised surprises will increase word of mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose costume appropriate to persona and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Costume should fit the performer and the trick; inappropriate ethnic or incongruous costumes can undermine the performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt attire to the performer’s strengths and to audience expectations: Talon abandoned a Chinese costume in favour of a magician's dress, which better suited his persona and the theatrical demands of the trick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruit and cultivate talented assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistants with natural aptitude can contribute tricks and stagecraft; selecting the right collaborators can raise the quality of the whole performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot helpers with innate 'genius des trucs' (e.g., Macalister) and engage them as stage partners; train and allow them to create repertoire enhancements. Good collaborators may enable more ambitious presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build robust props and provide backups
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical or prop failure (e.g., a crayon breaking during an automaton drawing) can spoil a demonstration even if the device is otherwise excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure durable materials and redundancies for critical prop components; perform pre-show checks and have quick remedies (spare pencils, secondary mechanisms) so small faults do not derail the impression of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the audience through participation and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Involving spectators (children as participants, borrowed hats, audience objects) and spectacular visual variety (automata, animals, flowing objects) increases amusement and applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design segments that invite safe audience participation and that culminate in visually rich reveals (e.g., producing many objects from a hat, fish appearing in basins). Participant involvement should be rehearsed so it appears spontaneous and amusing rather than risky.
